models.name: CCGX WiFi module simple, Nano USB (BPP900100200)

gotchas: It is a USB WiFi stick, not a device. It has no protocol, no addresses, and no driver surface. It exists in this catalogue so that a future pass does not research it twice.

Carried by a vendor table: Cerbo GX manual, Internet connectivity — BPP900100200 'CCGX WiFi Module Simple (Nano USB)', 'Compact, low cost.' The same table lists BPP900200300 (Asus USB-N14, 'Higher cost; better reception than Nano USB') and BPP900200400 (WiFi module long range, Netgear AC1200, 'Supports Wireless AC, G,

Largely redundant on modern hardware — the Cerbo GX and Cerbo GX MK2 already have built-in WiFi; the manual lists Ethernet, built-in WiFi, mobile network and USB tethering as the four connection methods, with these dongles as range extenders. Its live use is an older CCGX or a GX sited badly.
Do not confuse with cellular. The same manual page: 'The Cerbo GX does not support mobile broadband USB dongles, except for the official GX GSM and GX LTE 4G accessories.'
unmappedReports: Nothing of its own. Worth knowing where the nearest thing lives: the HOST GX exposes com.victronenergy.platform Network/Wifi/SignalStrength, documented in Victron's Venus D-Bus wiki as 'Normalized value of the wifi signal strength. Value is between 0 and 100', alongside Network/Wifi/State ('ready', 'online', 'idle', 'association', 'configuration') and Network/Services. That percent value would map cleanly onto link-signal-quality — note the contrast with the GX LTE modem's 0–31 scale., Network/Wifi/State is a five-value connection state with no MetricKind and no ValueKind; RunState is the wrong domain., com.victronenergy.platform HAS registers in the Modbus TCP workbook — but only 5800–5812, the VE.Bus backup/restore block. No networking registers at all. Verified by parsing the committed workbook. So even the WiFi signal strength is MQTT-only.
